figures.label: Figure 1
figures.caption: ASPIRE system overview. A coordinator spawns an actor agent (coding agent) per task, enabling parallel learning across tasks. Each actor refines and validates robot programs through iterative debugging with the robot execution engine, which exposes per-primitive multimodal traces for failure attribution and repair. Evolutionary search samples diverse candidate programs ($\pi_{0},\ldots,\pi_{k}$), sends each through the engine, and conditions the next generation ($\pi^{\prime}_{0},\ldots,\pi^{\prime}_{k}$) on surviving programs and residual failure traces. The coordinator writes validated repairs into a shared skill library, which future actors retrieve as in-context guidance; skills discovered in simulation can also be adapted as cross-embodiment guidance for real-robot programming.
figures.headline: A coordinator assigns actor agents to tasks, and validated repairs go into a shared skill library that future actors retrieve.
citing_sentences: An overview of ASPIRE is shown in Fig. 1.
As shown in Fig. 1, ASPIRE adopts a coordinator–actor architecture.

figures.label: Figure 2
figures.caption: Robot execution engine. Trace-guided debugging on a BEHAVIOR-1K navigate-and-pick-up-radio task. (a) Ego-view keyframes and overlays show the robot locating the radio but failing to approach it. (b) The primitive trace localizes the failure to repeated PLANNING_ERRORs: candidate navigation goals fall inside the table’s collision-avoidance buffer. (c) The agent patches the program with a multi-angle approach routine, re-perceives the radio from a reachable side, and completes the grasp. The validated repair is admitted as a reusable Multi-Angle Approach skill.
figures.headline: Per-primitive traces localize a radio pickup failure to planner errors, and a multi-angle approach repair completes the grasp.
citing_sentences: Fig. 2 zooms in on one BEHAVIOR-1K navigate-and-pick-up-radio debugging episode.

For the radio task in Fig. 2, the admitted skill is a navigation recovery pattern rather than a complete radio-pickup program: when planner errors recur near an obstacle boundary because sampled target poses fall inside the collision buffer, sample alternative approach directions around the object before retrying perception and grasping.

figures.label: Figure 3
figures.caption: Skill library. ASPIRE stores validated, agent-discovered repair knowledge as reusable in-context skills rather than a fixed set of human-written primitives. Top: representative entries show learned skills about localization disambiguation, motion-primitive construction, and navigation recovery. Middle: the library grows across heterogeneous categories, including localization, navigation, motion primitives, object-level grasping, scene understanding, and debugging workflows. Bottom: selected skills discovered in simulation are used as in-context guidance for real-robot programming, providing evidence that skills can transfer across embodiments. Additional skill examples and prompts are shown in Appendix A.
figures.headline: The skill library grows across localization, navigation, motion, grasping, scene understanding, and debugging categories.
citing_sentences: Fig. 3 shows representative entries and the resulting library breadth.
This appendix expands the representative entries shown in Figure 3 into the skill-library taxonomy.

figures.label: Figure 4
figures.caption: ASPIRE improves over prior coding agents and end-to-end VLAs across three benchmark families. (a) Short-horizon manipulation on LIBERO-Pro; (b) contact-rich manipulation on Robosuite; (c) long-horizon mobile manipulation on BEHAVIOR-1K. ASPIRE evaluates one generated program per task across held-out seeds, while CaP-Agent0 regenerates a separate program per seed with test-time reasoning and retries. ASPIRE improves performance across all benchmarks, with several results surpassing programs written by human experts. Detailed per-task results are in Appendices B and E.1.
figures.headline: ASPIRE scores above prior coding agents and end-to-end policies on LIBERO-Pro, Robosuite, and BEHAVIOR-1K benchmarks.
citing_sentences: Figure 4 summarizes the main evaluation.
This section reports the exact numerical values visualized in Figure 4 of the main paper.

figures.label: Figure 5
figures.caption: Cross-task zero-shot transfer on LIBERO-Pro Long. Skills accumulated on LIBERO-90 improve zero-shot performance on held-out long-horizon tasks. Figure (a) compares the full $N{=}90$ library with baselines. Figure (b) shows success under position and task perturbations as the size of the skill library increases. All success rates are macro-averaged over 10 tasks per axis. Per-task results are in Appendix C.
figures.headline: Skills from LIBERO-90 transfer zero-shot, and success on held-out long-horizon tasks rises as the library grows.
citing_sentences: Figure 5(a) compares the full $N{=}90$ skill library with prior baselines on the two LIBERO-Pro Long transfer axes: ASPIRE reaches 23% success on position perturbations and 38% on task perturbations, outperforming CaP-Agent0 and $\pi_{0.5}$ on both axes.

Figure 5(b) shows that success increases consistently as the size of the skill library grows, indicating that validated repairs from short-horizon tasks provide reusable robotic knowledge for longer-horizon compositions.

figures.label: Figure 6
figures.caption: Solving a Rubik’s Cube on the real robot. (a) GPT-6 Astra positions both grippers, holds the cube, turns one layer, aligns the layers, and releases. (b) Time and tokens per completed turn fall across episodes as context and skills accumulate.
figures.headline: The real robot solves a Rubik's Cube, and time and tokens per completed turn fall across episodes as skills accumulate.
citing_sentences: Figure 6(a) shows one face turn, and Figure 6(b) shows end-to-end time per completed turn decreasing from 16 min 58 s to 7 min 48 s and 3 min 05 s. Across the first and final episodes, tokens per turn fall from 11.27 M to 2.01 M, and estimated model cost, at OpenAI API prices (OpenAI, 2026e), from \$16.85 to \$2.89.

figures.label: Figure 7
figures.caption: Robot execution engine and evolutionary search ablations on LIBERO-Pro. (a), (b) Stacked bars under position and task perturbation: the base system without the robot execution engine or evolutionary search, the gain from adding the engine, and the additional gain from evolutionary search. (c) Average progress over low-performing tasks across evolutionary-search iterations. Per-task results are in Appendix E.
figures.headline: Adding the execution engine and then evolutionary search raises LIBERO-Pro success under both perturbation types.
citing_sentences: Figure 7(a) and (b) decompose success by component.
Figure 7(c) tracks performance on low-performing tasks as the evolutionary-search budget increases.

figures.label: Figure 8
figures.caption: Model ablation: success versus cost. Held-out success versus estimated API cost per task (list prices, log scale) on the 10 LIBERO-Pro Goal tasks under the position perturbation, using ASPIRE iterative debugging without evolutionary search and with an initially empty skill library. Colors mark the model family; hollow markers are the open-weight Kimi K3 and Qwen 3.8 Max. The green line is the cost/success frontier: the models that no cheaper model outperforms, labeled with success and cost per task. The success axis is broken below 50% to show GPT-6 Luna (15%). All values are in Table 18; per-task results for Claude Opus 5, Opus 5.5, and GPT-6 Astra are in Appendix E.6.
figures.headline: Success on LIBERO-Pro Goal under position perturbation rises with model strength, from 15% for GPT-6 Luna to 99% for Claude Opus 5.5.
citing_sentences: On LIBERO-Pro Goal under the position perturbation (Figure 8), success rises from 15% with GPT-6 Luna and 56% with Claude Opus 4.6 to 99% with Claude Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5; the best open-weight model, Kimi K3, reaches 78%.

Weaker models such as GPT-6 Luna, Claude Opus 4.6, Qwen 3.8 Max, and GPT-6 Sol reach only 15–59% on LIBERO-Pro Goal under the position perturbation, and the best open-weight model, Kimi K3, reaches 78% (Figure 8); our best results use proprietary frontier models.
Because ASPIRE improves as the underlying model improves (Figure 8), we expect progress in frontier and open-weight models to ease several of these limitations.

figures.label: Figure 9
figures.caption: Model ablation on LIBERO-Pro. Held-out success per suite and perturbation (10 tasks $\times$ 50 seeds); hatched segments are the gain from evolutionary search (Opus 4.6 on Long without it). Unlike the empty-library runs in Figure 8, these runs carry the skill library across tasks within a suite, so their Goal values under position perturbation differ. Tables 3 and 4 (right) give the same comparison on BEHAVIOR-1K and Robosuite.
figures.headline: Newer models reach 96–99% on LIBERO-Pro Object, Goal, and Spatial with iterative debugging alone, against 62% for Opus 4.6.
citing_sentences: With Claude Opus 5, Opus 5.5, or GPT-6 Astra (Figure 9; Tables 3 and 4), iterative debugging alone reaches 96–99% on LIBERO-Pro Object, Goal, and Spatial, against 62% for Opus 4.6 (72% with evolutionary search).

figures.label: Figure 10
figures.caption: Case study: five solvers, two tasks. Each row shows one episode: the human teleoperation demonstration from the original LIBERO dataset, and one held-out evaluation episode of the ASPIRE program written by each model. Frames run left to right in time and are labelled with the step they show. Percentages are held-out success over 50 seeds (Table 26); the demonstrations all succeed. Green and red borders mark the shown episode’s success or failure. The plate demonstration uses the original, unblocked layout. Two more tasks are in Appendix F.
figures.headline: Stronger models change strategy on the book and plate tasks, while weaker models keep the default grasp-and-move approach and fail.
citing_sentences: Figure 10 compares how four models and a human solve two tasks.

figures.caption: Debugging skills. Representative skill-library entries that encode reusable debugging strategies, including failure signatures, when-to-apply guards, and validated repair sketches.
figures.headline: Debugging entries record failure signatures, when-to-apply guards, and validated repair sketches.

figures.headline: Localization entries ground ambiguous object references into perception and localization routines.

abstract: Abstract: Traditional robot programming is notoriously challenging: it requires orchestrating multimodal perception, managing complex physical contact dynamics, and handling diverse environment configurations and execution failures. We introduce ASPIRE (Agentic Skill Programming through Iterative Robot Exploration), a continual learning system for robotics that autonomously writes and refines robot control programs in a code-as-policy paradigm while compounding experience into a reusable skill library. ASPIRE enables automated discovery of reusable skills that persist across multiple tasks, simulation and real-world settings, and different embodiments. Rather than relying on fixed, human-engineered pipelines, ASPIRE operates in an open-ended learning loop, consisting of three key components: (1) a closed-loop robot execution engine that exposes fine-grained multimodal traces (e.g., perception overlays, grasp candidates, motion trajectories, and collision feedback), enabling the agent to autonomously diagnose failures, synthesize repairs, and validate outcomes; (2) a continually expanding skill library that distills validated fixes into reusable, transferable robotic knowledge; and (3) an evolutionary search procedure that generates diverse programs, systematically debugging them to explore beyond single-trajectory refinement. As ASPIRE encounters more tasks, its growing skill library enables increasingly rapid adaptation. Consequently, ASPIRE surpasses prior methods by up to 77% on manipulation tasks under perturbation, 72% on Robosuite’s bimanual handover task, and up to 32% on long-horizon household tasks. The accumulated skill library further enables strong zero-shot generalization: on representative unseen long-horizon tasks, ASPIRE achieves 31% success, substantially outperforming the 4% success rate of prior methods despite their heavy reliance on test-time reasoning and retries. Performance scales with the capabilities of frontier models. With Claude Opus 5.5, ASPIRE nearly saturates these benchmarks, achieving 99% average success across all 80 LIBERO-Pro tasks and 100% success on representative Robosuite and BEHAVIOR-1K tasks. Beyond simulation, skills discovered in simulation reduce real-world robot programming effort across embodiments and robot APIs, while skills acquired through online interaction with physical robots enable ASPIRE to solve a Rubik’s Cube with progressively improving efficiency.

sections.body: Existing robot coding agents receive only coarse task-level feedback, and they discard discovered fixes after each task. ASPIRE adds three parts: a closed-loop execution engine that records per-primitive multimodal traces, a skill library of validated repairs, and an evolutionary search over candidate programs. The paper reports that ASPIRE improves success over prior coding agents by up to 77%, reaches 99% average success across all 80 LIBERO-Pro tasks with Claude Opus 5.5, and reaches 31% zero-shot success on LIBERO-Pro Long versus 4% for prior coding agents.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: ASPIRE lets a coding agent write and repair robot programs from fine-grained traces and reuse validated fixes across tasks.

sections.body: ASPIRE has three parts: a robot execution engine that records per-primitive traces and runs repairs, a skill library, and an evolutionary search over candidate programs. In the radio example, perception returns a pose, but repeated navigation calls return `PLANNING_ERROR` because the target lies within about 20 cm of a table edge. The actor writes a multi-angle approach routine as the repair. A fresh verifier must reproduce the source task's success before a skill is admitted. Evolutionary search samples K candidates per round and stops at a success threshold θ on debug seeds or after T rounds. A coordinator also orders tasks as a curriculum.
sections.heading: Method
sections.headline: A coordinator dispatches actor agents whose validated repairs are admitted to a shared skill library after verifier checks.

sections.body: The main coding agent is Claude Opus 4.6 in Claude Code, with one generated program per LIBERO-Pro and Robosuite task evaluated on held-out seeds. Averaging position and task perturbations, ASPIRE gains 77% on Object, 41.5% on Goal, and 42.5% on Spatial over the strongest baseline in each LIBERO-Pro suite. On Robosuite, bimanual handover rises from 20% to 92%. On BEHAVIOR-1K, navigate-and-pick-up-radio task success rises from 56% to 88%. On the real bimanual robot, skill retrieval lifts soda-can lifting from 65% to 95% success. The section also reports that success depends on the underlying model, and the model ablation compares twelve models.
sections.heading: Experiments
sections.headline: ASPIRE beats prior coding agents and end-to-end policies on three benchmarks, rising from 20% to 92% on bimanual handover.

sections.body: Prior robot control work includes end-to-end vision-language-action policies and executable programs that compose perception, planning, and control interfaces. Software-engineering agents supply a write-execute-debug loop for code. Work on self-improving agents uses open-ended memory, skill libraries, and self-evolving skill repositories, and other systems use language models to generate rewards, curricula, or candidate searches. The section states that ASPIRE differs by storing validated repair knowledge extracted from attributed embodied failures, rather than success-only memories, textual reflections, or reward functions. Its skills are reused as in-context guidance for future program repair.
sections.heading: Related Work
sections.headline: Related work spans end-to-end robot policies, executable robot programs, and skill libraries, where ASPIRE stores attributed repair knowledge.

sections.body: **Real-world autonomy:** a human still gives initial task guidance, scrambles the cube, and resets the scene between Rubik's Cube episodes. **Dependence on the model:** performance depends on a frozen language model, and the best results use proprietary frontier models. **Predefined interface:** the agent cannot express behaviors outside the exposed perception, planning, and control primitives without humans extending the interface. **Skill management:** a verifier checks a skill once at admission, so entries may become stale, redundant, or misleading for later tasks. **Compute cost:** debugging and evolutionary search consume many model calls and simulator or robot rollouts per task.
sections.heading: Limitations
sections.headline: Stated limits include dependence on a frozen language model, a fixed robot interface, one-time skill checks, and manual real-world resets.

sections.body: The conclusion states that ASPIRE outperforms existing end-to-end and coding-agent baselines, transfers zero-shot to unseen long-horizon tasks, and improves with the underlying model. With Claude Opus 5.5 it reaches 99% average success across all 80 LIBERO-Pro tasks and 100% on representative Robosuite and BEHAVIOR-1K tasks. On three real-robot tasks, skills discovered in simulation reduce real-robot programming token cost despite a different embodiment and robot interface. Skills learned online let GPT-6 Astra solve a Rubik's Cube on a real bimanual robot.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: ASPIRE pairs execution traces and evolutionary search with a growing skill library, reaching 99% average success on LIBERO-Pro with Claude Opus 5.5.

sections.body: Appendix A expands the skill-library entries shown in Figure 3, with the problem, when-to-apply guard, repair snippet, and origin task for each. Appendix B gives main benchmark tables, including a Robosuite mean of 68.0% for CaP-Agent0 and 81.0% for ASPIRE. Appendix C reports zero-shot transfer to LIBERO-Pro Long by library size, with per-task breakdowns. Appendix D describes the harness that connects a coding agent to a real robot through a tool interface. Appendix F covers case-study success rates, and Appendix G lists the pipeline prompt files and skill files in the public code repository.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: The appendix lists skill-library entries, benchmark tables, zero-shot and per-task results, the real-robot harness, and case-study details.
